question: What is a render prop in React?

options.text: A prop that accepts a function which the component calls to get JSX
options.explanation: Exactly: the component receives a function via a prop, calls it (passing the needed data), and embeds the result in its render.

options.text: An HOC function that accepts a component and returns a new component
options.explanation: This describes a Higher-Order Component (HOC), not a render prop. HOC wraps a component, render prop passes a render function.

options.text: A special React attribute for controlling component rendering
options.explanation: There is no special attribute. Render prop is a design pattern, not a built-in React feature.

options.text: A lifecycle method called before rendering
options.explanation: This describes shouldComponentUpdate or getSnapshotBeforeUpdate, not render prop. Render prop is a pattern of passing a function via props.

question: Why can't you use hooks inside a render prop callback?

options.text: Because the callback is a regular function, not a React component, and the rules of hooks don't apply
options.explanation: Hooks can only be used inside React functional components or custom hooks. A callback in a render prop is just a function called inside another component.

options.text: Because the render prop callback executes asynchronously
options.explanation: Render prop callbacks are called synchronously inside the component's render function. The reason hooks are forbidden is different: the callback is not a React component.

options.text: Because hooks only work in class components
options.explanation: On the contrary: hooks only work in functional components, not class components. But hooks also cannot be used in callback functions.

options.text: The restriction was lifted in React 18 — hooks now work in any function
options.explanation: This is incorrect. The rules of hooks haven't changed in React 18: hooks can still only be used in functional components and custom hooks.

question: You are building a DataList<T> component. How do you correctly declare the renderItem prop type?

options.text: renderItem: Function
options.explanation: The Function type is too broad: it doesn't describe either arguments or return value. The compiler won't warn about errors inside the callback.

options.text: renderItem: (item: object) => ReactNode
options.explanation: object is too broad — you can't access its fields without type casting. Generic T preserves the specific type of array elements.

options.text: renderItem: (item: any) => JSX.Element
options.explanation: any destroys type safety: TypeScript won't check that you're accessing existing fields of item. Use generic T.

options.text: renderItem: (item: T, index: number) => ReactNode
options.explanation: Exactly: the generic parameter T is used in the item type, allowing TypeScript to automatically infer the type from the data array.

question: In which situations is a render prop preferable to a custom hook? Select all that apply.

options.text: Creating a UI primitive (Headless UI, Radix) with full render control
options.explanation: Headless component libraries actively use render props (or compound components) to give the consumer full control over markup.

options.text: The component manages a limited DOM area (mouse tracking zone, drop zone)
options.explanation: When logic is tied to a specific DOM element (onMouseMove, onDrop), render prop gives the component control over its container, while a hook works globally.

options.text: You need to reuse fetch request logic between components
options.explanation: For reusing logic without UI — use hooks. useFetch/useQuery are much more convenient and don't create JSX nesting.

options.text: You need multiple render functions (renderItem, renderEmpty, renderHeader)
options.explanation: Multiple named render props are a natural way to give the consumer control over different parts of a single component's UI.

question: How does function-as-children differ from a named render prop?

options.text: A named render prop makes the function's purpose obvious without reading documentation
options.explanation: renderItem clearly says the function renders a list item. children as a function requires knowledge of the component to understand what it does with it.

options.text: Function-as-children works faster due to React reconciler specifics
options.explanation: There is no performance difference. Both variants call the function synchronously during render.

options.text: With function-as-children it's impossible to pass multiple render functions
options.explanation: A component has only one children. If you need renderItem + renderEmpty + renderHeader — you'll have to use named props.

options.text: Function-as-children is passed via children, a named one via an explicit prop
options.explanation: The key syntactic difference: <Comp>{fn}</Comp> vs <Comp render={fn} />. Both patterns call the function the same way.

question: What happens if you pass a render prop as a JSX tag instead of calling it as a function?

options.text: The render prop will be called as a component — this is an acceptable usage
options.explanation: This is not acceptable. When a prop is called renderItem (lowercase), React won't call it as a component. Use a function call: renderItem(item).

options.text: React will throw an error: components must start with a capital letter, and the prop is lowercase
options.explanation: React treats lowercase tags as HTML elements. <renderItem /> will try to create an HTML element 'renderItem', which leads to a warning and incorrect render.

options.text: Everything will work — React automatically understands it's a function
options.explanation: React doesn't auto-detect functions. <renderItem /> is not the same as renderItem(). These are different operations.

options.text: TypeScript won't allow compiling such code
options.explanation: TypeScript may pass this with a warning, but not necessarily an error — depends on settings. The error will occur at runtime.

question: You have a Toggle with a render prop. You need to add open/close animation via the useAnimation hook. How to do this correctly?

options.text: Use useEffect inside the render callback to start the animation
options.explanation: useEffect is also a hook, it cannot be called inside a callback. The rule applies to all hooks: only in components and custom hooks.

options.text: Add useAnimation inside the Toggle itself
options.explanation: Toggle is a generic component, it shouldn't know about animation. This violates the inversion of control principle: the consumer loses control over animation.

options.text: Call useAnimation directly inside the Toggle's render callback
options.explanation: Violation of hook rules: a callback in render prop is not a React component. React can't track hook call order in regular functions.

options.text: Create a separate AnimatedContent component and use useAnimation inside it, passing it as renderItem
options.explanation: Hooks can only be used in components. Extracting logic into a separate component is the correct pattern. AnimatedContent receives isOpen and calls useAnimation.

question: How do you declare a generic function in a TSX file so that <T> is not treated as a JSX tag?

options.text: Rename the file to .ts instead of .tsx
options.explanation: In .ts files there's no JSX, and <T> won't be ambiguous. But then you can't write JSX — not a solution for a component with JSX.

options.text: const DataList = <T>(props: DataListProps<T>) => ... — arrow functions don't have this problem
options.explanation: Arrow functions have the same problem in TSX! const DataList = <T> will be treated as the start of a JSX tag. The same comma is needed: <T,>.

options.text: function DataList<T,>(...) — add a comma after T
options.explanation: The comma is the standard way to disambiguate in TSX: <T,> cannot be a JSX tag, only a generic parameter.

options.text: function DataList<T extends object>(...) — add an extends constraint
options.explanation: Adding extends anything (object, unknown, {}) unambiguously tells TypeScript this is a generic parameter, not a JSX tag.

question: A MouseTracker component tracks the mouse via onMouseMove on a container. A user complains that coordinates update even when the mouse is outside the area. What's the problem?

options.text: The developer attached the handler to window instead of the container
options.explanation: If mousemove is attached to window or document, events will come from everywhere. onMouseMove on a div container limits tracking to that element's area.

options.text: The browser problem — onMouseMove is always global
options.explanation: This is incorrect. onMouseMove in React works via event bubbling, but if attached to a specific div — events only come when the mouse moves over that element and its descendants.

options.text: You need to use onMouseEnter instead of onMouseMove
options.explanation: onMouseEnter fires only on entering the element, not on movement. This won't solve the problem and is unsuitable for coordinate tracking.

options.text: The component didn't clean up the event subscription in useEffect
options.explanation: If onMouseMove was used via JSX attribute (not addEventListener in useEffect), cleanup is not needed — React manages this automatically.

question: What is better to pass to a Toggle render prop: only isOpen, or the full group { isOpen, toggle, open, close }?

options.text: Pass setIsOpen directly — so the consumer gets full control
options.explanation: Passing setState directly is bad practice: the consumer can set invalid state or break component invariants. Better to pass named action functions.

options.text: The full group { isOpen, toggle, open, close } — the consumer chooses what to use
options.explanation: A rich API gives the consumer flexibility: a dropdown uses toggle, a modal uses open/close separately, expandable uses only toggle. Passing only isOpen shifts state management to the consumer.

options.text: Only isOpen — fewer props, cleaner API
options.explanation: If you pass only isOpen, the consumer can't change state — they don't have access to setIsOpen. You need to pass control functions too.

options.text: Only toggle — the consumer only needs to toggle state
options.explanation: For a modal you need separate open and close: the open button calls open, clicking the overlay calls close. toggle doesn't always fit.
